finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.trigger: Attacker-controlled input can be injected into the interface string
finding.assumptions: The interface variable could potentially be set from user input or an external source

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked that the 'interface' variable is assigned a compile‑time constant string "eth0" on line 21; no user input, environment variable, command‑line argument, or external source is used. Therefore there is no path from an untrusted source to the setsockopt call. No additional checks or code paths can introduce untrusted data here.

finding.title: Buffer Overflow
finding.untrusted_source: inet_pton with a hardcoded IP address
finding.trigger: If the IP address string is longer than expected, it could overflow the buffer
finding.assumptions: The IP address could be dynamically set from an untrusted source

parsed.refutation_attempt:
1) Not a source of untrusted data: the IP string is a hard‑coded literal, not from stdin, a file, network, argv, env var, IPC, or caller‑supplied API.
2) Even if the string were longer, inet_pton writes exactly sizeof(struct in_addr) bytes and returns an error; no unchecked copy is performed.
3) No path exists from an untrusted input to the inet_pton call.

finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.trigger: If the IP address string is modified by an attacker, it could lead to command injection
finding.assumptions: The IP address could be modified by an attacker

parsed.refutation_attempt: The source of the IP address is a compile‑time string literal "192.168.1.2" (line 31), not an untrusted input such as stdin, argv, or a network source. The printf on line 38 simply prints this literal and the interface string; there is no path that allows an attacker to influence the format string or the data passed to printf. Thus there is no command injection risk.
